title: Rational polyhedral cones have finite rational half-space descriptions
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q$-vector space [def-weil-field] [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], let $v_1,\ldots,v_m\in V$ (allowing $m=0$), and put $C=\{\sum_j q_jv_j:q_j\in\mathbf Q_{\ge0}\}$. Then there are finitely many $\mathbf Q$-linear forms $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s:V\to\mathbf Q$ (allowing $s=0$) such that $$C=\{x\in V:\lambda_i(x)\ge0\text{ for every }i\}.$$ This is the rational Minkowski--Weyl (finite H-cone) description; no pointedness or spanning hypothesis is required.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 3.1.29, printed p. 103, rational polyhedral-cone description; Kato 1994, Toric singularities, is WANTED for a proof of the finite rational half-space form.

proof.text: By [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], choose a finite spanning list in $V$. Repeatedly remove an element expressible as a linear combination of the others; the span is unchanged and the list strictly shortens. The resulting list $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ is linearly independent: any nontrivial relation, solved for a vector with nonzero coefficient, would allow another removal. It is therefore a basis. For $x=\sum_h x_he_h$ let $\epsilon_h(x)=x_h$. Uniqueness of coordinates shows $\epsilon_h(x+y)=\epsilon_h(x)+\epsilon_h(y)$ and $\epsilon_h(qx)=q\epsilon_h(x)$, so these are rational linear forms. Their signed family $\{\epsilon_h,-\epsilon_h:1\le h\le n\}$ has nonnegative locus $\{0\}$, because both signs force every coordinate to be zero. For $V=0$ this family is empty.

source.place: Agent-written proof, base family: finite coordinates and the zero cone. Remark 3.1.29 is contextual only and does not contain this argument.

proof.text: For $0\le k\le m$ put $C_k=\{\sum_{j=1}^k q_jv_j:q_j\in\mathbf Q_{\ge0}\}$. We prove by induction on $k$ that $C_k$ is the nonnegative locus of a finite family of rational linear forms. The preceding signed coordinate family gives the base case $C_0=\{0\}$. For the induction step, suppose $C_k=\{x:f_i(x)\ge0\ (i\in I)\}$ for a finite index set $I$, and put $v=v_{k+1}$. Splitting off the last coefficient gives $$x\in C_{k+1}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists t\in\mathbf Q,\ t\ge0\ \text{and}\ f_i(x)-t f_i(v)\ge0\ (i\in I).$$ Indeed the old inequalities say exactly that $x-tv\in C_k$.

source.place: Agent-written proof, induction assertion, base case and coefficient identity. Remark 3.1.29 is contextual only and does not contain this argument.

proof.text: Set $a_i=f_i(v)$ and partition $I$ as $I_0=\{i:a_i=0\}$, $I_+=\{i:a_i>0\}$, $I_-=\{i:a_i<0\}$. Define a new family $\mathcal F$ consisting of $f_h$ for $h\in I_0$, $f_i$ for $i\in I_+$, and $$g_{ij}=a_i f_j-a_j f_i\qquad(i\in I_+,\ j\in I_-).$$ It is finite, since the old index set and its indicated product are finite, and every member is rational linear. Steps 4 and 5 verify that its nonnegative locus is exactly $C_{k+1}$; thus this defines the induction step without assuming a separation or cone-duality theorem.

source.place: Agent-written proof, explicit next finite family. Remark 3.1.29 is contextual only and does not contain this argument.

proof.text: Suppose $x\in C_{k+1}$ and choose $t\ge0$ as in Step 2. For $h\in I_0$, $f_h(x)=f_h(x)-ta_h\ge0$. For $i\in I_+$, $f_i(x)=(f_i(x)-ta_i)+ta_i\ge0$. For $i\in I_+$ and $j\in I_-$, cancellation gives $$g_{ij}(x)=a_i(f_j(x)-ta_j)+(-a_j)(f_i(x)-ta_i)\ge0,$$ since both coefficients are positive. Hence every form in $\mathcal F$ is nonnegative at $x$.

source.place: Agent-written proof, forward inclusion by cancellation. Remark 3.1.29 is contextual only and does not contain this argument.

proof.text: Conversely, suppose all forms in $\mathcal F$ are nonnegative at $x$. The finite nonempty set $B=\{0\}\cup\{f_j(x)/a_j:j\in I_-\}\subset\mathbf Q$ has a largest member $T$, obtained by successively taking the larger of two entries. Thus $T\ge0$. For each $i\in I_+$, the inequality $f_i(x)\ge0$ gives $0\le f_i(x)/a_i$, and for each $j\in I_-$ the inequality $g_{ij}(x)\ge0$ gives $$\frac{f_j(x)}{a_j}\le\frac{f_i(x)}{a_i}.$$ Here division reverses the inequality precisely because $a_i a_j<0$: the displayed difference is $g_{ij}(x)/(a_i a_j)\le0$. Every entry of $B$ is consequently at most $f_i(x)/a_i$, so $T\le f_i(x)/a_i$. It follows that $f_i(x)-Ta_i\ge0$ for $i\in I_+$. For $j\in I_-$, $T\ge f_j(x)/a_j$, and multiplication by $a_j<0$ gives $f_j(x)-Ta_j\ge0$. For $h\in I_0$ the same inequality is just $f_h(x)\ge0$. Thus $x-Tv\in C_k$ and $T\ge0$, so Step 2 gives $x\in C_{k+1}$.

source.place: Agent-written proof, reverse inclusion with an explicit rational coefficient. Remark 3.1.29 is contextual only and does not contain this argument.

proof.text: Steps 3--5 construct the required finite family for $C_{k+1}$ from that for $C_k$, completing the induction. At $k=m$ we have $C_m=C$, and enumeration of the final family gives the forms $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s$ of the statement. All operations used rational coefficients, with division only by the strictly signed $a_i$. Empty sign classes cause no problem: $B$ always contains $0$, and if $I_+$ is empty there are no upper bounds to satisfy. If the old family is empty then the new one is empty and both cones are $V$. For $m=0$ the signed coordinate family applies, and for $V=0$ the empty family applies for every $m$. No pointedness or spanning assumption on the given generators was used.

source.place: Agent-written proof, induction conclusion and degenerate cases. Remark 3.1.29 is contextual only and does not contain this argument.
